claim: On 5 January 2024 Alaska Airlines flight 1282, a Boeing 737-9 (N704AL), lost its left mid exit door plug in climb after takeoff from Portland
source_quote: On January 5, 2024, a Boeing 737-9 airplane operated by Alaska Airlines as flight 1282 experienced an in-flight separation of the left mid exit door (MED) plug and rapid depressurization when climbing through about 14,830 ft after takeoff from Portland International Airport

claim: The cabin pressure dropped at 17:12:33 as the airplane climbed through about 14,830 feet; the cabin altitude warning came on, then the master caution 1 second later
source_quote: at 1712:33, the airplane was climbing through about 14,830 ft when the cabin pressure dropped, and the cabin altitude warning activated, followed 1 second later by the master caution alert
note: p. 2; times PST. Spec said 16,000 ft: wrong

claim: The airplane reached a maximum of 16,320 feet at 17:13:41, about a minute after the event, then descended
source_quote: at 1713:41, the airplane reached its maximum altitude of 16,320 ft then began to descend (about 1 minute after the cabin pressure had dropped)

claim: It landed back at Portland at 17:26:46, about 14 minutes after the plug separated
source_quote: FDR data showed that the flight landed at 1726:46, about 14 minutes after the MED plug separated

claim: One flight attendant and 7 passengers had minor injuries; the 2 pilots, 3 flight attendants and 164 passengers were uninjured
source_quote: One flight attendant and 7 passengers received minor injuries; the captain, the first officer, 3 flight attendants, and 164 passengers were uninjured

claim: The captain called it an explosive experience; the first officer said it was chaos
source_quote: The captain described the rapid depressurization event as “an explosive experience,” and the first officer stated, “it was chaos.”

claim: The cockpit voice recorder held no audio from the accident flight
source_quote: The cockpit voice recorder (CVR) recording contained no audio from the accident flight
note: p. 1 fn 3; no cockpit audio exists to use

claim: Seats 26A and 26B, next to the plug, were empty
source_quote: seats 26A and 26B were unoccupied

claim: The plug is about 29 inches wide and 59 inches high
source_quote: An MED plug is a rectangular airframe structure, about 29 inches wide and 59 inches high

claim: The plug weighs 63 pounds at 1 g
source_quote: The nominal weight of the MED plug at 1.0 g was 63 lbs.

claim: Twelve stop fittings, six on each side, stop the plug moving outward: stop pins bear against stop pads
source_quote: The MED plug is also equipped with 12 stop fittings (6 on each vertical side) such that, in the plug’s installed position, the plug’s stop fittings align inboard of corresponding stop fittings on the fuselage frame and prevent the plug from moving outboard

claim: Four bolts stop the plug moving upward: two upper guide track bolts and two vertical movement arrestor bolts, each with washers, a castle nut and a cotter pin
source_quote: The four bolts that secure an MED plug from moving upward vertically are installed in the following locations: One upper guide track bolt is installed through each upper guide fitting below the upper guide roller. Each bolt installation (with two washers) is secured with a castle nut and cotter pin.
note: p. 12; vertical movement arrestor bolts same page

claim: When lifted far enough to open, the stop fittings clear the stop pads by about half an inch
source_quote: At the point where the plug’s upper guide fittings clear the upper guide rollers, the plug’s stop fittings have cleared the stop pads by about half an inch

claim: One vertical movement arrestor bolt alone would have prevented upward movement; the two upper guide track bolts alone would have kept the plug on its stops
source_quote: an installation with only one vertical movement arrestor bolt (with both upper guide track bolts and the other vertical movement arrestor bolt missing) was capable of preventing upward movement of the MED plug
note: p. 33; Boeing engineering review cited by NTSB. The design margin: four where one would hold

claim: None of the four bolts were found, and the bolt holes showed no bolt contact damage: the bolts were missing before the plug moved
source_quote: the absence of bolt contact damage or deformation around the holes associated with the vertical movement arrestor bolts and upper guide track bolts indicates that the four bolts that should have been installed to prevent the left mid exit door plug’s upward movement were missing before the plug moved upward off the stop pads

claim: The plug crept upward in small steps over previous flights, then on the accident flight rose off its stops and left the airplane
source_quote: The left mid exit door plug displaced incrementally upward during previous flights; then, during the accident flight, it displaced upward to the point of stop pin to stop pad instability, then upward, outboard, and aft as it separated from the fuselage.

claim: Parallel dark lines of dust, dirt and petroleum jelly near the upper seal recorded the plug's step-by-step rise
source_quote: These lines were evidence that the left MED plug had moved incrementally upward during previous flight cycles.

claim: On the sister plug with its bolts out, a 120-pound pull did not move it; two people pushing with an estimated 150-plus pounds did
source_quote: An upward force of 120 lbs was applied (to the limits of the gauge) with no vertical movement of the plug. Additional force by two people, estimated to exceed 150 lbs, was applied, and the plug moved vertically upward

claim: In flight, vertical loads dipped as low as 0.40 to 0.45 g, an effective plug weight of about 25 pounds
source_quote: The 0.40–0.45 g level represented an effective plug weight of 25 lbs.
note: p. 33; from 106,008 values over 9 flights, error about +/-0.15 g

claim: Vibration and flexing in normal flight likely walked the plug upward
source_quote: it is likely that dynamic loads imparted by the vibrations and flexing associated with normal flight operations led to the gradual and incremental upward movement of the left MED plug

claim: The extra gap at the plug's lower edge before it let go was about half an inch, not readily detectable on a walkaround
source_quote: the evidence of the upward displacement of the left mid exit door plug before the accident flight would not have been readily detectable by a flight crewmember performing a routine preflight walkaround inspection

claim: The airplane was delivered to Alaska Airlines on 31 October 2023 and had flown 154 cycles
source_quote: Alaska Airlines took delivery of the accident airplane from Boeing on October 31, 2023, and placed it into service on November 11, 2023. At the time of the accident, the airplane had accumulated 510 hours and 154 cycles.

claim: Spirit AeroSystems in Wichita closed the plug with all four bolts on 28 July 2023; the fuselage reached Boeing's Renton plant on 31 August 2023
source_quote: Records showed that Spirit AeroSystems personnel in Wichita completed the final closure of the left MED plug on July 28, 2023, which, per the specified production order, included installing the two upper guide track bolts and two vertical movement arrestor bolts

claim: On 1 September 2023 Boeing found five damaged rivets in the frame just forward of the plug
source_quote: Boeing personnel identified workmanship discrepancies with five rivets in the edge frame forward of the left MED plug

claim: Spirit staff were not allowed to remove completed installations; only Boeing personnel could open the plug
source_quote: Per Boeing’s manufacturing process, Spirit AeroSystems personnel were not authorized to remove completed installations on a fuselage to access a work area; only Boeing personnel were allowed to perform such work.

claim: A first rivet fix on 6 September was stamped as done but the rivets had only been painted over
source_quote: Boeing quality assurance personnel documented that the rivets were not removed and replaced but “just painted over.”

claim: On 17 September a message in Boeing's tracking tool said: if removal needed, a removal needs to be written first
source_quote: The entry stated, “If removal needed, a removal needs to [be] written first.”

claim: On 18 September at 07:00 the door manager said the door is being opened by mechanic
source_quote: the Boeing door manager indicated that the “door is being opened by mechanic.”

claim: Opening the plug required a removal record under Boeing's process; none was ever created
source_quote: No removal record for opening the left MED plug was identified in CMES, and Boeing’s search of all other available record sources identified no evidence that one had been created.

claim: The plug was open from at least the morning of 18 September until at least 17:09 on 19 September 2023
source_quote: The investigation determined the left MED plug was open at least as early as 1053 on September 18, 2023, and remained open until at least 1709 on September 19, 2023
note: p. 48 (p. 87 gives 1035 for the earliest: say 'that morning')

claim: The most experienced door team member, about 25 years on 737 doors, was on leave both days
source_quote: the most experienced door team member who was typically tasked with opening an MED plug, should the need arise, was unavailable to assist because he was on leave that day and the next day

claim: None of the door team on duty had ever opened a plug, and no one said they knew who opened it
source_quote: Neither the door team manager nor any of the door team personnel on duty when the left mid exit door (MED) plug was opened had any experience with opening an MED plug, and none said they had any knowledge of who opened it.

claim: A technician later found the plug lying open on a stand and strapped it up and let it hang
source_quote: He said he “just strapped it up there and let it hang,” leaving a gap around it in the frame.

claim: The plug was closed on the evening shift of 19 September, when no door team member was on duty
source_quote: Only door team personnel were allowed to perform work on doors and mid exit door (MED) plugs, but none were on duty at the time the left MED plug was closed.

claim: Text messages between Boeing workers included a photo sent about 18:39 showing the plug closed with no attachment hardware in the three visible locations
source_quote: The texts included a photograph sent about 1839 that showed the plug in a closed position with no attachment hardware in the three locations visible (see figure 18).
note: p. 51; Figure 18 is the key exhibit (Source: Boeing, cropped by NTSB)

claim: Who closed the plug was never identified
source_quote: None of the manufacturing personnel who provided a statement or participated in an interview indicated knowledge of who performed the final closure of the plug.

claim: With no removal record, no quality inspection of the plug closure was performed
source_quote: Due to the absence of a removal record indicating that the left mid exit door plug installation had been disturbed, no quality assurance inspection of the plug closure was performed.

claim: The inspector's sign-off on 20 September did not involve looking at the airplane
source_quote: stated that her signoff did not involve looking at the airplane but rather verifying that all the steps on the IP related to the rivet rework had been signed off

claim: Boeing's parts-removal instruction ran to more than 50 pages and listed more exceptions than directions
source_quote: the BPI was more than 50 pages long and contained several hyperlinks to various other instructions for determining which process was applicable and when it should be followed. It listed more exceptions about when the removal process was not needed than guidance indicating when it was.

claim: Boeing revised that instruction 11 times between 2013 and 2023, and it featured in 16 regulatory compliance issues from 2018 to 2023
source_quote: From 2013 to 2023, Boeing substantively revised BPI “Perform Part or Assembly Removal” 11 times
note: p. 62; 16 issues p. 63 (9 voluntary disclosures, 7 FAA compliance actions)

claim: Boeing's corrective actions, accepted by the FAA, failed to fix a problem documented for at least 10 years
source_quote: Although accepted by the Federal Aviation Administration, Boeing Commercial Airplanes’ corrective actions were ineffective to address the persistent deficiencies with Boeing’s Business Process Instruction “Perform Part or Assembly Removal,” which had a documented history of compliance issues for at least 10 years before the accident.

claim: The 737 line built about 52 airplanes a month before 2018, fewer than 10 at the pandemic low, and about 30 to 38 before the accident
source_quote: Before 2018, Boeing produced about 52 airplanes per month from its Boeing 737 production line. During the height of the pandemic slowdown after 2020, production was less than 10 airplanes per month but had increased to about 30 to 38 airplanes per month before the accident.

claim: After the two fatal 737 MAX accidents Boeing cut production, halted hiring and did not replace staff who left; the pandemic took more, particularly retirement-eligible employees
source_quote: in 2018 and 2019, following two fatal accidents involving Boeing 737 MAX airplanes, the company significantly decreased production of the airplane. This required reallocating personnel and halting the hiring process, including not replacing personnel lost through attrition. In 2020, the global pandemic resulted in further workforce reductions, particularly among retirement-eligible employees

claim: In 2022 Boeing set out to return to pre-2018 production and hired many people with no manufacturing experience
source_quote: In 2022, Boeing sought to increase production to pre-2018 levels and increased hiring to compensate for the employees lost. During that time, Boeing hired people, many of whom had no previous manufacturing experience.

claim: Boeing's 737 general manager: ten years ago close to 50 percent of employees had more than ten years' experience; now 25 or 30 percent
source_quote: “…10 years ago, we were closer to 50% of employees with more than 10 years’ [experience]. Today, I would say we are at 25 or 30%..., certainly a shift in… tremendous experience level.”
note: p. 57; attribute to Boeing's VP and GM of the 737 program

claim: Boeing did not assess the risk of using a less experienced workforce
source_quote: Because Boeing Commercial Airplanes did not conduct a change management assessment to identify and address the risks associated with using a workforce with reduced experience, including hiring many with little or no previous manufacturing experience, it missed an opportunity to proactively implement mitigations to ensure quality standards were maintained.

claim: The NTSB could not assess whether adverse pressure existed on the production line
source_quote: an assessment of Boeing’s safety culture, including whether adverse pressure existed on the production line, could not be performed as part of this investigation
note: finding 27: fairness limit. Say this in the film.

claim: Five FAA inspectors were assigned to the 737 program while the fuselage was at Renton
source_quote: Five FAA inspectors were assigned to the Boeing 737 production program at the time the accident airplane’s fuselage was in the Renton facility.

claim: The FAA's 68 alleged noncompliances at Renton from October 2022 to September 2023 never referenced the removal instruction
source_quote: From October 2022 to September 2023, FAA inspectors documented 68 alleged noncompliances identified during audit activities at Boeing’s Renton facility; however, none referenced BPI “Perform Part or Assembly Removal.”

claim: NTSB probable cause: Boeing's failure to provide adequate training, guidance and oversight for its parts removal process; contributing: the FAA's ineffective oversight
source_quote: the probable cause of this accident was the in-flight separation of the left mid exit door (MED) plug due to Boeing Commercial Airplanes’ failure to provide adequate training, guidance, and oversight necessary to ensure that manufacturing personnel could consistently and correctly comply with its parts removal process
note: p. 122; quote the full text on screen

claim: The report was adopted on 24 June 2025 as AIR-25-04
source_quote: Aviation Investigation Report AIR-25-04 June 24, 2025

claim: Boeing's quality chief told a June 2024 media briefing the move crew closed the plug; the NTSB said interviews did not identify who closed it and cut Boeing off from investigative information for the unauthorized release
source_quote: we notified Boeing that we would not tolerate such violations of regulations and the NTSB party agreement and that we would no longer provide Boeing access to the investigative information we continued to produce

claim: In 2005 Boeing's Wichita, Tulsa and McAlester operations became Spirit AeroSystems
source_quote: In 2005, Spirit Holdings became a standalone Delaware company, and commenced operations through the acquisition of Boeing’s operations in Wichita, Kansas, Tulsa, Oklahoma, and McAlester, Oklahoma (the “Boeing Acquisition”).

claim: About 64 percent of Spirit's 2023 revenue came from Boeing
source_quote: For the twelve months ended December 31, 2023, approximately 64% and 19% o f our net revenues were generated from sales to Boeing and Airbus, respectively.

claim: Spirit made the plug in Malaysia and installed it in Wichita; the fuselage arrived at Renton with the plug in place
source_quote: The Spirit AeroSystems facility in Malaysia manufactured the accident airplane’s left MED plug on March 24, 2023

claim: In December 2018 Boeing's board approved a share repurchase plan of up to 20 billion dollars
source_quote: On December 17, 2018 , the Board approved a repurchase plan for up to $20 billion of common stock.
note: Boeing 10-K for 2019. Context only: no record links buybacks to the accident (money_trail_notes.md)

claim: Boeing repurchased 9.0 billion dollars of its shares in 2018 and 2.7 billion in 2019, then suspended repurchases
source_quote: During 2019 and 2018 we repurchased 6.9 million and 26.1 million shares totaling $2.7 billion and $9.0 billion through our open market share repurchase program.
note: Boeing 10-K for 2019; 'Share repurchases under this plan are currently suspended.'

claim: In its 2022 annual report Boeing said the 737 program struggled to stabilize production at 31 a month and planned to increase rates
source_quote: The 737 program has experienced operational and supply chain challenges stabilizing production at 31 per month.

claim: Boeing's 2023 annual report: the 737 was being produced at 38 a month
source_quote: We are currently producing at a rate of 38 per month.

claim: On 24 January 2024 the FAA told Boeing it would not grant any production expansion of the MAX
source_quote: The FAA today informed Boeing it will not grant any production expansion of the MAX, including the 737-9 MAX.

claim: FAA Administrator Whitaker: This won't be back to business as usual for Boeing
source_quote: “However, let me be clear: This won’t be back to business as usual for Boeing.

claim: 171 Boeing 737-9s were grounded until their plugs were inspected
source_quote: The inspections required by Emergency AD 2024-02-51, which affected 171 Boeing 737-9 airplanes

claim: Boeing agreed on 30 June 2024 to buy Spirit AeroSystems back
source_quote: On June 30, 2024, The Boeing Company (the “ Company ”) entered into an Agreement and Plan of Merger (the “ Merger Agreement ”), by and among Spirit AeroSystems Holdings, Inc.

claim: Boeing completed the acquisition of Spirit AeroSystems on 8 December 2025
source_quote: On December 8, 2025, The Boeing Company (the “Company”) issued a press release announcing the completion of its acquisition of Spirit AeroSystems Holdings, Inc

claim: Boeing and Spirit developed a fix: two secondary retention devices and lanyards on the bolts, expected in new production in 2026
source_quote: Boeing stated that, once the design enhancement is certified, installation in all applicable new production airplanes would likely begin sometime in 2026

claim: NTSB member Inman: this could have resulted in tragedy if the event had taken place over the Pacific
source_quote: As I mentioned in the Board meeting, this could have resulted in tragedy if the event had taken place over the Pacific.

claim: NTSB member Graham: skeptical Boeing's systems were equipped to catch these errors
source_quote: I am skeptical Boeing’s systems at the time were equipped to catch these types of errors and would have successfully prevented a similar accident.

claim: Boeing kept factory security video for 30 days, so none existed for the build
source_quote: No Boeing security video recordings of the accident airplane’s build process were available. Boeing maintained such recordings for 30 days, and the accident occurred after this period.

claim: The photograph of the closed plug was taken 108 days before the plug left the airplane (19 September 2023 to 5 January 2024)
source_quote: Text messages between Boeing personnel discussing interior restoration after the rivet rework was completed provided evidence that the left MED plug was closed during second shift operations that day
note: Our calculation from C35 (19 Sep 2023, about 1839) and C01 (5 Jan 2024): 11 + 31 + 30 + 31 + 5 = 108 days

claim: The 737-9 has an opening in each side aft of the wing for an extra emergency exit; airlines that do not need it get a plug, a lighter and less complex option
source_quote: Per design, the Boeing 737-9 is equipped with a rectangular opening on each side of the fuselage aft of the wing that can accommodate the installation of an emergency exit door when required for certain passenger seating configurations.
note: pp. 10-11; 'an MED plug can be installed as a lower weight, less complex option'

claim: Faint washer outlines around the upper bolt holes showed the hardware had been installed at one time
source_quote: Faint outlines associated with the upper guide track bolt washers were observed around the upper guide track bolt holes, indicating that hardware was installed at one time.

claim: Spirit AeroSystems is a major supplier of Boeing 737 fuselages
source_quote: Spirit AeroSystems, one of the world's largest manufacturers of aerostructures for commercial airplanes, business and regional jets, and defense aircraft platforms, is a major supplier of Boeing 737 and 787 fuselages to The Boeing Company.

claim: A removal record ensures a disturbed installation is restored to its engineering requirements, listing the steps and the quality signoffs
source_quote: The removal record listed the steps that needed to be performed to restore the disturbed installation back to an accepted status, per the applicable engineering requirements, and it specified any signoffs from manufacturing personnel, quality assurance inspectors, or both associated with each step, as well as the final quality assurance signoff.

claim: The request for access was elevated twice to raise management visibility
source_quote: SAT entries documented that the request was elevated twice to increase management visibility of the issue

claim: When the inspection was signed off on 20 September, the cabin sidewalls were already installed over the plug; the airplane was delivered 41 days later
source_quote: The records showed that IP “OK to Install Blankets” was signed off as completed on September 20, 2023. At that point, the accident airplane’s interior sidewalls had already been installed over the left MED plug.
note: pp. 52-53; 41 days = our calculation from 20 Sep to 31 Oct 2023 (C22)

claim: The upper guide fittings split where the rollers punched through them, and the lower hinge fittings show a twisting load as the plug went out
source_quote: Fracture patterns on the lower hinge guide fitting attachment bolts and flanges had overstress features indicative of a twisting load having been imparted on the lower hinge guide fittings.
note: pp. 84-85; rollers 'contacting and punching through the walls at the inboard side of each guide track'

claim: Boeing's quality chief told a June 2024 media briefing: we know the move crew closed the plug
source_quote: we believe the move crew; we know the move crew closed the plug.
note: p. 52 fn 60; Boeing SVP of quality, 25 Jun 2024 media briefing

claim: Boeing's internal audits on other production lines in 2024 still found problems with unauthorized part removals
source_quote: repeated findings for failure to prevent unauthorized removals (March 2024)
note: p. 64; other production lines; also 'ineffective internal controls for part removals (May 2021 and February 2024)'

claim: The emergency airworthiness directive grounding the 737-9s for plug inspections was issued on 6 January 2024
source_quote: Based on the preliminary investigative findings for this accident, on January 6, 2024, the FAA issued Emergency AD 2024-02-51 to prohibit the further flight of all Boeing 737-9 airplanes until the MED plugs were inspected

claim: Opening the plug was a nonroutine task; no door team member with that experience was on duty when it was opened or closed
source_quote: However, opening an MED plug was a nonroutine task, and no personnel experienced with opening or closing an MED plug were on duty at the times that the accident airplane’s left MED plug was opened and closed

claim: NTSB member Graham noted Boeing had taken at least 20 actions before the report was published
source_quote: Prior to these recommendations formally being issued, and prior to this report’s publication, Boeing has taken at least 20 actions
note: p. 127, board member statement (balance: the company's response)

claim: The cockpit voice recorder kept recording after landing and the accident flight's audio was overwritten
source_quote: By the time maintenance personnel responded to the airplane to pull the CVR circuit breaker, the audio for the accident flight had been overwritten.

claim: Boeing repurchased 2.7 billion dollars of stock in 2019 and its repurchases were suspended by the time of its 2019 annual report (filed January 2020)
source_quote: Share repurchases under this plan are currently suspended.
note: Boeing 10-K for 2019; the 2018 purchases ($9.0B) and the December 2018 authorization in C56-C57

claim: The NTSB report does not mention buybacks or share repurchases
source_quote: an assessment of Boeing’s safety culture, including whether adverse pressure existed on the production line, could not be performed as part of this investigation
note: Absence verified by full-text search of AIR-25-04 (no 'buyback', 'repurchase', 'dividend', 'share price'); quote is finding 27, said beside it

claim: Spirit said the contract mechanic who recorded the rivets as replaced had confused the airplane with another
source_quote: He stated that he had confused [the accident] airplane with another airplane he was working on that day.
note: p. 47; Spirit's senior manager at the NTSB hearing, 6 Aug 2024

claim: Recorded cabin pressure (CPC1) fell from about 14.1 psi to about 8.4 psi within about 5 seconds of 17:12:33 PST
source_quote: Pacific Standard Time,...,CPC1 Cabin Press,CPC2 Cabin Press,... (psi)
note: FDR tabular data, docket attachment 1; resampled 1 s values 14.0938 → 8.3750 psi between 17:12:32 and 17:12:38 (remotion/data/fdr_1282.json). Data, not prose: the quote is the column header

claim: Cabin pressure loads push the plug radially outward, carried through its 12 stop fittings
source_quote: The pressure loads (radially outward) are carried through 12 stop fittings on the MED plug, 6 on each side
note: NTSB Structures Group Chair's Factual Report §1.1 (answers the audience panel's 'why didn't pressure jam it' question)

claim: To open, the plug moves vertically upward with a slight inboard inclination until the stops clear the pads, then pivots outboard about the lower hinge bolts
source_quote: the initial MED plug motion for opening is vertically upward at a slight inclination inboard such that the plug stops will clear the fuselage stop pads. Once clear, the MED plug pivots outboard about the lower hinge fitting bolts.

claim: Boeing's tracking tool is the Shipside Action Tracker (SAT)
source_quote: Shipside Action Tracker
note: report acronym list; on screen in Act III escalation

claim: The functional test technician's second shift on 18 Sep 2023 ran 1330 to 2330; the plug's position was undetermined 1710–1838 on 19 Sep and it was closed during second shift
source_quote: who worked second shift on September 18, 2023 (1330 to 2330)
note: Act III plug-status chart; second shift drawn 13:30–23:30 on 19 Sep (same shift pattern); undetermined 1710–1838 quoted from the same page

claim: The left MED plug's position was undetermined between 1710 and 1838 on 19 September 2023
source_quote: The left MED plug’s position was undetermined on September 19, 2023, between 1710 and 1838
